state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's clarify the misconception here. Changing all values by the same proportion will impact the range. To see this, let's consider how the range is calculated and how it changes when the values are adjusted. Can you explain why changing all the plant heights by the same proportion would or would not affect the range?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, so the range is like the difference between the biggest and smallest number, right? So if I cut all the plants in half, like 42 becomes 21 and 13 becomes 6.5, then the difference would be 21 minus 6.5 which is 14.5... but the original range was 42 minus 13 which is 29. So that's different! Does that mean Tom is actually wrong too?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Great job in working through the example! You're correct that changing all the plant heights by the same proportion does indeed affect the range. Just like how adjusting the heights by cutting them in half changed the range, increasing them all by the same amount would also alter the range. So, Katie's statement about the range not changing if all the plants grew by 3 cm each is also incorrect. Keep in mind that the range is sensitive to changes in the data values.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively engages the misconception and the student demonstrates clear improvement in reasoning, but the teacher makes a critical mathematical error in Turn 3 by incorrectly stating that adding a constant to all values changes the range (it doesn't), which undermines the domain accuracy despite good pedagogical approach.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher uses questioning to elicit student reasoning rather than directly explaining with worked examples, and makes a critical mathematical error in Turn 3 by incorrectly stating that adding a constant changes the range, which contradicts traditional teaching's emphasis on clarity and accuracy.
